Pluck a string and you get a note you could hum. Strike a drum and you get a thud. Both are a stretched piece of material, set shaking. So why do they sound so different?


## The answer in three steps

**1. Everything that vibrates has a set of favorite shapes.** A string can swing as one arc, as two halves moving in opposite directions, as three thirds, and so on. Each of these shapes, called a [mode](glossary.qmd#mode), swings at its own frequency.

```{=html}
<svg class="fig" viewBox="0 0 320 112" role="img" aria-label="The first three modes of a string: one arc, two halves, three thirds, at 1, 2 and 3 times the lowest frequency"><path class="dash" d="M 40 22 L 280 22"/><path class="acc" d="M 40 22 C 126.4 7.7 193.6 7.7 280.0 22"/><path class="acc" opacity="0.35" d="M 40 22 C 126.4 36.3 193.6 36.3 280.0 22"/><circle cx="40" cy="22" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="280" cy="22" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><text x="290" y="26">1×</text><path class="dash" d="M 40 56 L 280 56"/><path class="acc" d="M 40 56 C 83.2 41.7 116.8 41.7 160.0 56 C 203.2 70.3 236.8 70.3 280.0 56"/><path class="acc" opacity="0.35" d="M 40 56 C 83.2 70.3 116.8 70.3 160.0 56 C 203.2 41.7 236.8 41.7 280.0 56"/><circle cx="40" cy="56" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="280" cy="56" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><text x="290" y="60">2×</text><path class="dash" d="M 40 90 L 280 90"/><path class="acc" d="M 40 90 C 68.8 75.7 91.2 75.7 120.0 90 C 148.8 104.3 171.2 104.3 200.0 90 C 228.8 75.7 251.2 75.7 280.0 90"/><path class="acc" opacity="0.35" d="M 40 90 C 68.8 104.3 91.2 104.3 120.0 90 C 148.8 75.7 171.2 75.7 200.0 90 C 228.8 104.3 251.2 104.3 280.0 90"/><circle cx="40" cy="90" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="280" cy="90" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><text x="290" y="94">3×</text></svg>
```

**2. A pluck sets many of them going at once.** What you hear is a mix of the modes' frequencies: the lowest, called the [fundamental](glossary.qmd#fundamental), and the [overtones](glossary.qmd#partial) above it. They are the stems on the ruler above.

**3. Whether that mix sounds like one note depends on how the frequencies line up.** If they are all, or very nearly, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the range we hear as pitch, the sound repeats itself at the largest such frequency, many times a second, and the ear hears that repetition rate as the [pitch](glossary.qmd#pitch). A string's modes do exactly that: 1×, 2×, 3×, …. An ideal drumhead's land at 1×, 1.59×, 2.14×, 2.30×, …: a few fall near a line by chance, but no frequency we hear as pitch fits them all. The sound doesn't repeat at any rate we hear as pitch, and it dies fast: a thud. Drums with a clear note, such as the timpani (kettledrums), are built so that one set of their modes lands near the lines and the rest are weak or fade fast (page 8).

::: {.northstar}
**The idea behind the whole series.** Apply Newton's law to a small piece of an instrument and you get a rule for how its shape is pulled back toward rest: its [operator]. The shapes that rule only scales up or down are the modes; each swings at its own frequency, and left to ring, the instrument moves as a mix of them. The operator's [spectrum](glossary.qmd#spectrum) fixes those frequencies, so it decides what the instrument can sound like: **on the lines, a note; off the lines, a clang or a thud.**
:::

[Skip to the journey ↓](#the-journey)

## One instrument from each class

Musicologists sort instruments into five classes by what makes the sound ([Hornbostel–Sachs](glossary.qmd#hornbostel-sachs)): strings, air, solid bodies, stretched skins and electric circuits. Here is one of each, playing Grieg.

The two drums show the series' answer in miniature. An ideal drumhead's frequencies are off the lines, so the bass drum booms without a clear pitch; a kettledrum is built so that one set of its modes lands near the lines and the others fade fast, so it plays a note ([page 8](drum.qmd#one-drumhead-two-drums)).

## The mathematics in one example

The smallest instrument with more than one mode is two beads on a tight string, with both ends tied. Pull one bead aside and let go, and both beads wobble in a tangled way that never quite repeats. But two ways of starting them are special. Lift both beads together, and they swing together forever, at one frequency. Lift one up and push the other down, and they swing in opposite directions forever, at √3 ≈ 1.73 times that frequency: now the stretch of string between the beads pulls too, so the restoring pull is three times as strong, and a frequency goes as the square root of the pull (page 1).

```{=html}
<svg class="fig" viewBox="0 0 320 112" role="img" aria-label="The two modes of two beads on a string with tied ends. Left: both beads move together, at the lower frequency. Right: they move in opposite directions, at about 1.73 times that frequency."><path class="dash" d="M 10 50 L 150 50"/><path class="acc" d="M 10 50 L 56.7 28 L 103.3 28 L 150 50"/><path class="acc" opacity="0.35" d="M 10 50 L 56.7 72 L 103.3 72 L 150 50"/><circle cx="56.7" cy="28" r="5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="103.3" cy="28" r="5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="56.7" cy="72" r="5" class="fillacc" opacity="0.35"/><circle cx="103.3" cy="72" r="5" class="fillacc" opacity="0.35"/><circle cx="10" cy="50" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="150" cy="50" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><text x="80" y="102" text-anchor="middle">together: 1×</text><path class="dash" d="M 170 50 L 310 50"/><path class="acc" d="M 170 50 L 216.7 28 L 263.3 72 L 310 50"/><path class="acc" opacity="0.35" d="M 170 50 L 216.7 72 L 263.3 28 L 310 50"/><circle cx="216.7" cy="28" r="5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="263.3" cy="72" r="5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="216.7" cy="72" r="5" class="fillacc" opacity="0.35"/><circle cx="263.3" cy="28" r="5" class="fillacc" opacity="0.35"/><circle cx="170" cy="50" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="310" cy="50" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><text x="240" y="102" text-anchor="middle">opposite: 1.73×</text></svg>
```

These two shapes are the beads' modes, and every motion of the two beads, the tangled one included, is a mix of them, each part swinging at its own frequency. The rule that turns the beads' heights into the pulls on them is their operator; a mode is a shape that the rule only scales; the numbers that fix the modes' frequencies form its spectrum. A string, a column of air, a steel bar and a drumhead are the same story with more and more small pieces, each pulled back by its own rule. [Page 2](ring.qmd) works the two beads out in full, and [the spectrum of an operator](spectrum.qmd) proves that every free motion is a mix of modes and says where that stops being exact: when a bow or a breath keeps driving the motion, when the swings are large, or when friction mixes the modes.

## Did instrument makers know?

Not in these terms. Instruments came first, shaped over centuries by trial and ear; the mathematics came later and explained them, from Mersenne's laws of vibrating strings (1636) and d'Alembert's wave equation (1747) to Rayleigh's *The Theory of Sound* (1877). Designing an instrument by computing its spectrum is recent: a carillon bell with a major third in its overtones, where traditional bells have a minor third, was designed by computer at the Eindhoven University of Technology for the Eijsbouts bell foundry; the [map](map.qmd#did-instrument-makers-know) tells the longer story.

[operator]: glossary.qmd#operator

```{=html}
<ol class="journey">
  <li class="part">The idea</li>
  <li><a href="note.html"><span class="n">0</span><span class="t">What makes a sound a note?</span></a><span class="hint">When a sound's frequencies are all, or very nearly, whole-number multiples of one frequency, the sound repeats, or nearly repeats, at the largest such frequency, and if that rate is in the range we hear as pitch, the ear hears it as the pitch, even when that frequency itself is missing.</span><span class="controls"><button data-g="note">▶ The note</button><button data-g="nofund">▶ Without it</button></span></li>
  <li><a href="oscillator.html"><span class="n">1</span><span class="t">Why does a fading note stay in tune?</span></a><span class="hint">A mass on a spring vibrates at one frequency, √(k/m)/2π (k its stiffness, m its mass), and the size of the swing doesn't enter (for small swings), which is why a fading note keeps its pitch.</span></li>
  <li><a href="ring.html"><span class="n">2</span><span class="t">How can a tangled wobble be a few simple motions?</span></a><span class="hint">With many masses the operator is a table of numbers (a matrix); the shapes it only rescales (its eigenvectors) swing as independent springs, and any motion is a mix of them.</span></li>
  <li><a href="circle.html"><span class="n">3</span><span class="t">Why does a loop of string land exactly on the lines?</span></a><span class="hint">A loop of string vibrates at exactly 1, 2, 3, … times its lowest frequency, because each wave around it has a whole number of crests and all waves travel at the same speed.</span></li>
  <li><a href="spectrum.html"><span class="n">★</span><span class="t">The spectrum of an operator</span></a><span class="hint">Left to ring, an object vibrates as a mix of its modes; the operator fixes their frequencies, and playing sets only how strongly each sounds.</span></li>
  <li class="part">Instruments</li>
  <li><a href="violin.html"><span class="n">4</span><span class="t">Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?</span></a><span class="hint">A light touch at the middle drains every mode that moves under the finger and leaves the even modes, which stand still there: a note an octave up.</span></li>
  <li><a href="clarinet.html"><span class="n">5</span><span class="t">Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?</span></a><span class="hint">Air in a tube obeys the string's equation with different ends: a tube closed at one end has only odd multiples of its lowest frequency, so a clarinet sounds almost an octave below a flute of the same length and overblows an octave and a fifth higher.</span><span class="controls"><button data-g="flute">▶ Flute-like</button><button data-g="clar">▶ Clarinet-like</button></span></li>
  <li><a href="kalimba.html"><span class="n">6</span><span class="t">Why does a kalimba sound clean?</span></a><span class="hint">A bar clamped at one end has overtones off whole-number multiples (6.27×, 17.55×), yet a kalimba sounds clean because those overtones die within a fraction of a second (observed, not derived).</span><span class="controls"><button data-g="kal">▶ Kalimba tine</button></span></li>
  <li><a href="harmonica.html"><span class="n">6b</span><span class="t">Where did the harmonica reed's overtones go?</span></a><span class="hint">Blown, the reed swings just below its own lowest frequency and chops the air into identical puffs, so the steady sound has only whole-number multiples and the reed's off-line overtones are absent from it.</span><span class="controls"><button data-g="kal">▶ Plucked</button><button data-g="harm">▶ Blown</button></span></li>
  <li><a href="piano.html"><span class="n">7</span><span class="t">Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?</span></a><span class="hint">A piano wire's stiffness puts each overtone slightly above its whole-number multiple, so tuners stretch octaves to reduce the beating, a slow wobble in loudness, most at the ends of the keyboard.</span><span class="controls"><button data-g="oct">▶ Exactly 2 : 1</button><button data-g="str">▶ Stretched</button></span></li>
  <li><a href="drum.html"><span class="n">8</span><span class="t">Why does a drum thud?</span></a><span class="hint">An ideal drumhead's frequencies (1, 1.59, 2.14, … times the lowest) fit no pitch, so a plain drum thuds; on a kettledrum, the air the head pushes pulls one set of modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5, a note.</span></li>
```

```{=html}
<script src="core.js"></script>
<script>
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var C = Core, M = C.models;
  function fadeOut(buf, sec) { var d = buf.getChannelData(0), n = Math.floor(sec * buf.sampleRate); for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) d[d.length - 1 - i] *= i / n; return buf; }
  // ---- the opening pair: a plucked string and a struck drum, on the pitch ruler ----
  var HOOK = {
    string: { parts: function () { return M.violin.partials({ pluck: 0.2 }); }, f: 196, dur: 2.6, svg: "rulerString" },
    drum: { parts: function () { return M.drum.partials({ r: 0.35 }); }, f: 140, dur: 2.4, svg: "rulerDrum" }
  };
  function drawRulers() {
    Object.keys(HOOK).forEach(function (k) {
      C.stems(document.getElementById(HOOK[k].svg), HOOK[k].parts(), { W: 320, H: 96, rmax: 6, fs: 9, sw: 2.5, noOff: true });
    });
  }
  document.querySelectorAll("[data-hook]").forEach(function (b) {
    b.addEventListener("click", function () { var h = HOOK[b.getAttribute("data-hook")]; C.play(C.render(C.toHz(h.parts(), h.f), h.dur), 0.75); });
  });
  // ---- the six puzzles ----
  function harmonics(f, n, odd, skip1) { var out = []; for (var k = 1; k <= n; k++) { if (odd && k % 2 === 0) continue; if (skip1 && k === 1) continue; out.push({ f: f * k, amp: 1 / k, tau: 10 }); } return out; }
  // Octave puzzle: simplified stiff-string notes, only the lowest partials, so the tuner's 2 : 1 beat (C4's 2nd partial against C5) stands out.
  var BS = 0.0024, LOW = 261.63, P2 = Math.sqrt((1 + 4 * BS) / (1 + BS));
  function stiffNote(f1, amps) { return amps.map(function (a, i) { var n = i + 1; return { f: f1 * n * Math.sqrt((1 + BS * n * n) / (1 + BS)), amp: a, tau: 3 }; }); }
  var GWW = [2.53794399980, 3.65550971352, 5.17555935622, 6.53755744376, 7.24807786256, 9.20929499840, 10.5969856913, 11.5413953956, 12.3370055014, 13.0536540557, 14.3138624643, 15.8713026200];
  function gww() { return GWW.map(function (v, k) { return { f: 150 * Math.sqrt(v / GWW[0]), amp: 1, tau: 1.4 / (1 + 0.12 * k) }; }); }
  var G = {
    string: function () { return C.render(C.toHz(M.violin.partials({ pluck: 0.2 }), 196), 2.6); },
    drum: function () { return C.render(C.toHz(M.drum.partials({ r: 0.35 }), 140), 2.4); },
    note: function () { return fadeOut(C.render(harmonics(220, 8), 1.6), 0.3); },
    nofund: function () { return fadeOut(C.render(harmonics(220, 8, false, true), 1.6), 0.3); },
    flute: function () { return fadeOut(C.render(harmonics(343 / 1.2, 8), 1.6), 0.3); },
    clar: function () { return fadeOut(C.render(harmonics(343 / 2.4, 15, true), 1.6), 0.3); },
    kal: function () { return C.render(C.toHz(M.kalimba.partials(), 523.25), 2.4); },
    harm: function () { return fadeOut(C.render(C.toHz(M.harmonica.partials(), 523.25), 1.6), 0.3); },
    oct: function () { return C.render(stiffNote(LOW, [1, 0.7, 0.3]).concat(stiffNote(2 * LOW, [0.7, 0.25])), 4); },
    str: function () { return C.render(stiffNote(LOW, [1, 0.7, 0.3]).concat(stiffNote(2 * LOW * P2, [0.7, 0.25])), 4); },
    gA: function () { return C.render(gww(), 2.4); },
    gB: function () { return C.render(gww(), 2.4); }
  };
  document.querySelectorAll("[data-g]").forEach(function (b) {
    b.addEventListener("click", function () { C.play(G[b.getAttribute("data-g")](), 0.75); });
  });
  C.onTheme(drawRulers);
  drawRulers();
})();
</script>
```

```{=html}
// The orchestra: one instrument from each Hornbostel–Sachs class, drawn and played by orchestra.js.
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var O = window.Orchestra; if (!O) return;
  var fams = document.getElementById("oFams"), mute = {};
  O.FAM.forEach(function (f) {
    var b = document.createElement("button"); b.type = "button"; b.className = "chip"; b.setAttribute("aria-pressed", "true");
    b.style.setProperty("--c", "rgb(" + f.hue.join(",") + ")"); b.innerHTML = '<span class="dot"></span>' + f.inst;
    b.addEventListener("click", function () { mute[f.id] = !mute[f.id]; b.setAttribute("aria-pressed", mute[f.id] ? "false" : "true"); applyMute(f.id); if (!ctx) drawRest(); });
    fams.appendChild(b);
  });
  var cv = document.getElementById("oStage"), g = cv.getContext("2d"), timeEl = document.getElementById("oTime");
  var tlPerf = O.timeline(false), tlFull = O.timeline(true), cur = tlPerf, ctx = null, t0 = 0, raf = 0, fg = null;
  tlPerf.mute = mute; tlFull.mute = mute;
  var REST = O.beatToSec(8 * 16 + 4.15);
  function fit() {
    var full = document.fullscreenElement === cv, dpr = Math.min(2, window.devicePixelRatio || 1);
    var w = full ? Math.min(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight * 16 / 9) : cv.getBoundingClientRect().width;
    w = Math.max(320, Math.round(w * dpr)); cv.width = w; cv.height = Math.round(w * 9 / 16);
  }
  function drawRest() { O.drawAt(g, REST, cv.width, cv.height, tlPerf); }
  function mmss(x) { x = Math.max(0, Math.round(x)); return Math.floor(x / 60) + ":" + ("0" + x % 60).slice(-2); }
  function applyMute(id) { if (fg && ctx) fg[id].gain.setTargetAtTime(mute[id] ? 0 : 1, ctx.currentTime, 0.03); }
  function frame() {
    if (!ctx) return;
    var t = ctx.currentTime - t0;
    if (t > cur.dur) { stop(); return; }
    O.drawAt(g, Math.max(0, t), cv.width, cv.height, cur);
    timeEl.textContent = mmss(t) + " / " + mmss(cur.dur);
    raf = requestAnimationFrame(frame);
  }
  function stop() {
    cancelAnimationFrame(raf);
    if (ctx) { try { ctx.close(); } catch (e) {} }
    ctx = null; fg = null; timeEl.textContent = "Ready"; drawRest();
  }
  function play(full) {
    stop(); cur = full ? tlFull : tlPerf;
    var AC = window.AudioContext || window.webkitAudioContext;
    if (!AC) { timeEl.textContent = "This browser cannot play Web Audio."; return; }
    ctx = new AC(); if (ctx.resume) ctx.resume();
    var my = ctx; timeEl.textContent = "Computing the sounds…";
    setTimeout(function () {
      if (ctx !== my) return;
      var cache = O.prepare(ctx, cur.notes);
      t0 = ctx.currentTime + 0.2;
      fg = O.schedule(ctx, cur.notes, t0, { cache: cache, mute: mute });
      raf = requestAnimationFrame(frame);
    }, 30);
  }
  document.getElementById("oPlay").addEventListener("click", function () { play(false); });
  document.getElementById("oFull").addEventListener("click", function () { play(true); });
  document.getElementById("oStop").addEventListener("click", stop);
  var fsb = document.getElementById("oFs");
  if (!cv.requestFullscreen) fsb.hidden = true;
  fsb.addEventListener("click", function () { if (cv.requestFullscreen) cv.requestFullscreen().catch(function () {}); });
  document.addEventListener("fullscreenchange", function () { fit(); if (!ctx) drawRest(); });
  window.addEventListener("resize", function () { fit(); if (!ctx) drawRest(); });
  fit(); drawRest();
  var faces = ['700 48px "LM Roman"', 'italic 24px "LM Roman"', '24px "LM Roman"', '24px "LM Sans"', '24px "LM Math"'];
  if (document.fonts && document.fonts.load) Promise.all(faces.map(function (f) { return document.fonts.load(f, "A−κ♯"); })).then(function () { if (!ctx) drawRest(); }, function () {});
})();
</script>
```
